title: Hostile influence peddling, slopaganda style
gist: Dymples Leong argues the line between commercial AI slop and state propaganda ('slopaganda') is blurring: the same cheap generative content infrastructure and engagement-driven monetisation used for profit can be repurposed by hostile actors to flood information environments, as seen in campaigns targeting Australia, Singapore and Malaysia. Platform responses (labels, SynthID, spam removal) remain inconsistent while algorithms still reward AI content.

insights.claim: Australian researchers uncovered a foreign network of hundreds of Facebook pages with AI deepfakes impersonating Australian politicians, linked to a Sri Lankan influencer business, with 10% of pages monetised by Facebook.
insights.speaker: Dymples Leong
insights.so_what: Platforms are directly monetising influence networks, a reputational and regulatory risk for Meta.

insights.claim: Generative AI lets creators produce hundreds of videos or images at minimal cost while platform recommendation and monetisation systems reward attention, producing repetitive, inaccurate content that is not necessarily deliberately deceptive.
insights.speaker: Dymples Leong
insights.so_what: Engagement-based ad models structurally incentivise synthetic content flood.

insights.claim: The same commercial AI slop infrastructure used for profit can be repurposed by hostile state and non-state actors, who can disguise propaganda to be indistinguishable from commercial slop.
insights.speaker: Dymples Leong
insights.so_what: Attribution difficulty raises platform moderation costs and regulatory exposure.
insights.quote: The same infrastructure used by commercial actors for profit and financial gain, however, can be repurposed by hostile actors.

insights.claim: AI slop does not inherently signify an influence operation, but slopaganda can be a force multiplier within coordinated influence operations and election misinformation.
insights.speaker: Dymples Leong
insights.so_what: Distinguishes noise from targeted threats when assessing information risk.
insights.quote: AI slop does not inherently signify the presence of an influence operation.

insights.claim: Graphika research in 2025 found propaganda campaigns use AI for content creation and inauthentic influencer personas, including synthetic news reporters and AI-generated fake news sites.
insights.speaker: Dymples Leong
insights.so_what: Demand for detection and threat-intelligence services is growing.

insights.claim: In Singapore, hundreds of centrally coordinated YouTube videos spread false information about its foreign policy, economy and leadership, and AI-generated TikTok personas framed Singapore as economically reliant on China; Malaysia was also targeted.
insights.speaker: Dymples Leong
insights.so_what: State-linked narratives target perceptions of economic alignment in Southeast Asia.

insights.claim: Hostile actors need not fabricate controversies; they can amplify existing social, political or economic fault lines with enormous volumes of AI content.
insights.speaker: Dymples Leong
insights.so_what: Polarised markets are more vulnerable to sentiment manipulation.
insights.locator: A hostile actor seeking to influence

insights.claim: The objective of slop-based campaigns may be to shape the wider information environment via repeated exposure, fostering uncertainty and distrust rather than belief in a particular falsehood.
insights.speaker: Dymples Leong
insights.so_what: Erosion of trust in information affects institutional legitimacy and market sentiment.
insights.quote: Rather, the objective may instead be to shape the broader information environment in which citizens form opinions.

insights.claim: YouTube and LinkedIn are removing low-quality spam, Meta and TikTok apply automated AI labels, and more firms adopt SynthID detection, but enforcement is inconsistent and feeds still reward high-engagement AI posts.
insights.speaker: Dymples Leong
insights.so_what: Content-integrity tooling is a growth area but platform incentives remain misaligned.
insights.quote: However, enforcement across the platforms and products remains varied and inconsistent, while algorithmic feeds continue to reward AI-generated posts with high engagement rates.

insights.claim: A layered resilience approach is needed: government monitoring of recurring narratives and coordinated networks plus media and information literacy, going beyond merely detecting AI slop.
insights.speaker: Dymples Leong
insights.so_what: Points to policy demand for narrative-monitoring and literacy programmes.
